pages.title: Verification and handover
pages.for: The design predicts what each circuit should read. Compare a reading with the design, or with a limit, only at the same temperature. Before the tests, give the inspector each circuit's expected R1+R2 at the test temperature, its maximum Zs and where that comes from, the charts, anything a test could damage, and the supply's Ze and earthing: PME or PNB. At handover, give the client the certificate with its schedules, the charts, the notices and the records.
pages.rule:
R1+R2 is very nearly proportional to (temperature + 230 °C)
Factor from t1 to t2 = (t2 + 230) ÷ (t1 + 230)
Expected R1+R2 on the day = R1+R2 at 20 °C × (t + 230) ÷ 250
Expected Zs = Ze + expected R1+R2
Limit on the day = maximum measured Zs at 10 °C × (t + 230) ÷ 240
Zs hot = Ze + (R1+R2) ÷ test-day factor × operating multiplier

A cold reading should stay under 80% of Table 41.3.
A 90 °C cable near its rating: limit = Table 41.3 figure × (t + 230) ÷ 320.
A direct Zs usually reads lower than Ze + (R1+R2): parallel earth paths.
Like for like, readings usually come in a little under the design.
First periodic inspection: on the certificate. Commercial: 5 years.

traps.text: Setting a cold reading against the design's hot R1+R2 as it stands.
Moving a limit the wrong way: a warmer test day raises it.
Subtracting Ze from a direct Zs reading to find R1+R2.

pages.task: Remember the immersion heater circuit: 15 m of 1.5 mm² line and cpc. Its design R1+R2 is 24.2 × 1.2 × 15 ÷ 1000 = 0.436 Ω. You test it once it is installed, cold, on a 20 °C day. What should it read if the cable is as designed?
pages.why: The 1.2 takes the cable from 20 °C up to its running temperature. A cold test leaves it out. 24.2 × 15 ÷ 1000 = 0.363 Ω.

pages.name: What it is for
pages.text:
The design predicts what each circuit should read. Verification checks the installation against those figures before anyone uses it. It also checks each reading against its device's limit.

So the designer hands the inspector the figures to test against, worked for the temperature of the test. Then the client gets the certificate and the records to run the building safely.
pages.alt: The design predicts what each circuit should read. Verification checks the installation against those figures before anyone uses it. It also checks each reading against its device's limit. So the designer hands the inspector the figures to test against, worked for the temperature of the test. Then the client gets the certificate and the records to run the building safely. If it is skipped: Set a cold reading against a hot figure and it looks better than it is. It can pass a circuit that would fail when warm.
pages.html:
The design predicts what each circuit should read. Verification checks the installation against those figures before anyone uses it. It also checks each reading against its device's limit.

So the designer hands the inspector the figures to test against, worked for the temperature of the test. Then the client gets the certificate and the records to run the building safely.

If it is skipped: Set a cold reading against a hot figure and it looks better than it is. It can pass a circuit that would fail when warm.

pages.name: The why
pages.text: At 20 °C the cable reads 0.363 Ω. At 70 °C the same cable reads 0.436 Ω, the design's figure.
pages.alt: Design figure 70 °C Running hot 20 °C Resistance tables 10 °C Measured Zs limits 0.436 Ω Design at 70 °C Reading at 70 °C Factor from 20 °C 1.20 Reading 0.436 Ω At 70 °C the cable is as hot as the design assumed. So the reading meets the design at 0.436 Ω. Copper's resistance rises in step with its temperature plus 230 °C. So reading = 0.363 × (t + 230) ÷ 250, where t is the cable's temperature. Nothing about the cable changed. Only its temperature did. So compare a reading with the design only at one temperature. The same rule gives the factors you use for R1+R2 and Zs.
pages.html:
Factor from 20 °C1.20
Reading0.436 Ω

At 70 °C the cable is as hot as the design assumed. So the reading meets the design at 0.436 Ω.

Copper's resistance rises in step with its temperature plus 230 °C. So reading = 0.363 × (t + 230) ÷ 250, where t is the cable's temperature.

Nothing about the cable changed. Only its temperature did. So compare a reading with the design only at one temperature.

The same rule gives the factors you use for R1+R2 and Zs. From 20 °C up to 90 °C it is 320 ÷ 250 = 1.28. From 20 °C down to a 15 °C test day it is 245 ÷ 250 = 0.98.

The maximum measured Zs is the limit for a reading taken cold. It is the Table 41.3 figure divided by 1.25. That is 300 ÷ 240, from 70 °C down to 10 °C. So a cold reading should stay under 80% of the Table 41.3 figure. The 80% covers Ze too, though Ze does not warm with the cable. So the limit errs on the safe side.

pages.name: Check
pages.task: A 6 A type C circuit's limit for a reading at 10 °C is 2.91 Ω. You test it on a 25 °C day. What is the most it may read?
pages.why: A warmer cable reads higher, so the limit rises with it. The factor from 10 °C is (25 + 230) ÷ (10 + 230) = 1.06. Then 2.91 × 1.06 = 3.085 Ω.

pages.name: Worked example
pages.text: On a 20 °C day the heater should read about 0.573 Ω, and the most it may read is 2.271 Ω.
pages.alt: THE HEATER, TESTED ON A 20 °C DAY Expected R1+R2 = 24.2 × 15 ÷ 1000 = 0.363 Ω Expected Zs = 0.21 + 0.363 = 0.573 Ω Limit at 10 °C = 2.73 ÷ 1.25 = 2.184 Ω Factor from 10 °C to 20 °C = 250 ÷ 240 = 1.04 Limit on the day = 2.184 × 1.04 = 2.271 Ω Expect a reading near 0.573 Ω, often a little under. It passes while it stays under 2.271 Ω. You may remember the design as 0.43 Ω and 0.64 Ω. Those are the same hot figures, cut to two places.
pages.html:
The heater, tested on a 20 °C day

Expected R1+R2 = 24.2 × 15 ÷ 1000 = 0.363 Ω

Expected Zs = 0.21 + 0.363 = 0.573 Ω

Limit at 10 °C = 2.73 ÷ 1.25 = 2.184 Ω

Factor from 10 °C to 20 °C = 250 ÷ 240 = 1.04

Limit on the day = 2.184 × 1.04 = 2.271 Ω

Expect a reading near 0.573 Ω, often a little under. It passes while it stays under 2.271 Ω. You may remember the design as 0.43 Ω and 0.64 Ω. Those are the same hot figures, cut to two places.

pages.task: Parts 3(g) and 3(i) are both worked hot. Assume the tests are done on a 15 °C day. Take that as a practice value. On a real job, record the day's temperature. Your showroom: DBL2 and C7, ready to testScenario

A newly built car showroom, on a three-phase four-wire TN-C-S supply. Ze is declared as 0.1 Ω. A four-core SWA submain runs 20.0 m from the MDB to DBL2, the lighting board, on a 10 A type C breaker. Its armour is the cpc. C7 runs 23.8 m from DBL2 to the farthest walkway bollard. It is 1.5 mm² singles with a 1.5 mm² cpc, on a 6 A type C RCBO. The installation is finished and ready for its tests.

Carried forward
(g)Zs at DBL20.392 Ω
(i)Zs at C7's farthest bollard1.129 Ω

Parts 3(g) and 3(i) are both worked hot.

Assume the tests are done on a 15 °C day. Take that as a practice value. On a real job, record the day's temperature.

At 20 °C the submain's core is 4.61 mΩ/m and its armour 6.8 mΩ/m, over 20.0 m. C7's 1.5 mm² line and cpc are 24.2 mΩ/m over its 23.8 m.

Zs at C7's farthest bollard

Cold, the 15 °C dayHot, in serviceDesign0.887 Ωpart 4(a)1.129 Ωpart 3(i)As built?Ze + (R1+R2)?part 4(c)

Compare down a column, at one temperature.

Factor from 20 °C = (15 + 230) ÷ (20 + 230) = 0.98

Submain = (4.61 + 6.8) × 20.0 ÷ 1000 = 0.228 Ω, and 0.228 × 0.98 = 0.223 Ω

C7 = 24.2 × 23.8 ÷ 1000 = 0.576 Ω, and 0.576 × 0.98 = 0.564 Ω

Zs = 0.1 + 0.223 + 0.564 = 0.887 Ω

This is the figure you hand the inspector. The design's 1.129 Ω is the same circuit, hot.

These as-built readings are practice examples, not measurements. The submain's 10 A type C breaker has a Table 41.3 maximum of 2.19 Ω. Its limit for a reading at 10 °C is 1.75 Ω. The submain's 10 A type C breaker has a Table 41.3 maximum of 2.19 Ω. Its limit for a reading at 10 °C is 1.75 Ω.

Zs at C7's farthest bollard

Cold, the 15 °C dayHot, in serviceDesign0.887 Ωpart 4(a)1.129 Ωpart 3(i)As built0.842 ΩZe + (R1+R2)?part 4(c)

Compare down a column, at one temperature.

Give the limit in Ω. The comparison follows.

Factor from 10 °C = (15 + 230) ÷ (10 + 230) = 245 ÷ 240 = 1.02

Limit = 1.75 × 1.02 = 1.785 Ω

At DBL2, Ze + (R1+R2) = 0.08 + 0.214 = 0.294 Ω. The direct reading is 0.275 Ω. Both are far under 1.785 Ω, so they comply. The design expected 0.1 + 0.223 = 0.323 Ω.

C7's own limit, for its 6 A type C, is 2.91 × 1.02 = 2.968 Ω. At its far end, Ze + (R1+R2) = 0.08 + 0.214 + 0.548 = 0.842 Ω. The direct reading is 0.790 Ω. Both comply with plenty to spare.

These cold limits assume cables that run at up to 70 °C. C7 and the submain are 90 °C cables, but they carry a small share of their rating. So they run cool, and the 70 °C limits are fair here.

The direct reading comes in 0.052 Ω lower. A direct reading usually does, because it takes in parallel earth paths through bonded metalwork. So never subtract Ze from a direct reading to find R1+R2.

pages.name: Section A 4(c)

Zs at C7's farthest bollard

Cold, the 15 °C dayHot, in serviceDesign0.887 Ωpart 4(a)1.129 Ωpart 3(i)As built0.842 ΩZe + (R1+R2)1.076 Ωpart 4(c)

Compare down a column, at one temperature.

R1+R2 at 15 °C = 0.214 + 0.548 = 0.762 Ω

Back to 20 °C: 0.762 ÷ 0.98 = 0.778 Ω

Up to operating temperature: 0.778 × 1.28 = 0.996 Ω

Zs = 0.08 + 0.996 = 1.076 Ω

Like for like, the installation gives 1.076 Ω against the design's 1.129 Ω. That is 0.053 Ω lower, about 5%. Cold against cold, it is 0.842 Ω against the expected 0.887 Ω. That is 0.045 Ω lower.

Set the cold reading against the hot design and it looks 0.287 Ω lower. Most of that gap is only temperature.

Of the 0.053 Ω gap, 0.02 Ω is Ze. It measured 0.08 Ω against the declared 0.1 Ω. A declared Ze is a maximum, and so are the tabulated resistances. So readings usually come in a little under the design.

A reading well over the expected figure means something is wrong. The installation may differ from the design, such as a longer run or a poor connection. Or the test itself went wrong. Find out which.

pages.name: Handing over
pages.text:
Before the tests, the inspector gets five things. Each circuit's expected R1+R2 at the test temperature. Each circuit's maximum permitted Zs, and where it comes from if not Table 41.3. A chart or schedule of each circuit, with its points, its cable size and type, and its protective device. Anything a test could damage, such as SELV equipment. The supply's characteristics, including PME or PNB.

At handover, these go out. The Electrical Installation Certificate, which is valid only with its schedule of inspections and schedules of test results. The circuit charts and diagrams. The notices, including the periodic inspection notice at the origin. The O&M manual and building log book, where the contract asks for them. On a project under CDM, a copy of the certificate in the health and safety file. Where fixed building services need commissioning, a commissioning notice to building control and the owner.

You recommend the time to the first periodic inspection. It goes on the certificate. The recommended maximum is 5 years for commercial premises and 3 for industrial. The showroom is commercial, so take 5 years. Shorten it if the building will be poorly maintained or used harder than designed for. Cars on the floor are part of a showroom's normal use. They do not change the 5 years by themselves.

pages.name: Section B
pages.task: State what decides the maximum period to the showroom's first periodic inspection, and what you would recommend.
pages.why: A model answer: As the designer, I recommend the maximum period and enter it on the Electrical Installation Certificate. It allows for how often and how well the showroom will be maintained. It also allows for the type of installation, its use and the external influences on it, such as cars driven across the floor. The recommended maximum for commercial premises such as shops is 5 years. So I would recommend 5 years, or less if maintenance will be poor. It is a recommendation made by engineering judgement and agreed with the installer and others, not a fixed rule.

pages.name: Section B 2
pages.task: List three items of information a designer should give the inspector before the showroom's tests.
pages.why: A model answer: Before the tests I would give the inspector each circuit's expected R1+R2, worked for the test temperature. I would give each circuit's maximum permitted Zs, and say where it comes from if not Table 41.3. I would give a chart of each circuit, with its points, its cable size and type, and its protective device. I would flag anything a test could damage, such as SELV equipment. And I would give the supply's characteristics, such as the declared Ze of 0.1 Ω. I would say whether the TN-C-S supply is PME or PNB.

pages.name: Changed numbers
pages.task: A 25 A type C radial circuit is tested on a 20 °C day. It reads Zs 0.74 Ω. Table 41.3 gives 0.87 Ω. Its limit for a reading at 10 °C is 0.70 Ω. Determine the most it may read on the day, and state whether it complies.
pages.why: 250 ÷ 240 = 1.04; 0.70 × 1.04 = 0.728 Ω; a 0.74 Ω reading does not comply, though under 0.87 Ω
pages.alt: A 25 A type C radial circuit is tested on a 20 °C day. It reads Zs 0.74 Ω. Table 41.3 gives 0.87 Ω. Its limit for a reading at 10 °C is 0.70 Ω. Same method, new numbers. Give the limit in Ω. Factor = (20 + 230) ÷ (10 + 230) = 250 ÷ 240 = 1.04 Limit = 0.70 × 1.04 = 0.728 Ω 0.74 Ω is over 0.728 Ω, so it does not comply. Yet it is under 0.87 Ω. Set against the hot figure, it would have passed. The cold limit scales Ze too, though Ze does not warm with the cable. So it errs a little on the safe side. A reading over it still fails.
pages.html:
A 25 A type C radial circuit is tested on a 20 °C day. It reads Zs 0.74 Ω. Table 41.3 gives 0.87 Ω. Its limit for a reading at 10 °C is 0.70 Ω.

Same method, new numbers. Give the limit in Ω.

Factor = (20 + 230) ÷ (10 + 230) = 250 ÷ 240 = 1.04

Limit = 0.70 × 1.04 = 0.728 Ω

0.74 Ω is over 0.728 Ω, so it does not comply. Yet it is under 0.87 Ω. Set against the hot figure, it would have passed.

The cold limit scales Ze too, though Ze does not warm with the cable. So it errs a little on the safe side. A reading over it still fails.
